Good morning. I hope everybody has had a good morning and a good evening rest. Excellencies, distinguished participants, I hereby declare open the fourth meeting of the 61st session of the Human Rights Council. Excellencies, distinguished participants, we will now begin the high-level panel discussion On the commemoration of the 25th anniversary of the adoption of the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action held pursuant to Council Resolution 60/16. Following information received from the Secretary General on accessibility services for the 61st session, this panel discussion, as with the panel yesterday, is accessible through international sign interpretation and real-time captioning, together with other measures. As reflected in the letter I received from the Chef de Cabinet of the Secretary-General, which has been uploaded to the extranet, the provision of mandated accessibility services for panel discussions and for the interactive dialogue with the Special Rapporteur on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities is guaranteed for this session. It is my honour to welcome to the podium Ms. Nada Al-Nashif, Deputy High Commissioner for Human Rights, who will deliver an opening statement. It is also my honour to welcome Our distinguished panelists, Mr. Martin Chungong, Secretary General of the Inter-Parliamentary Union, Ms. Beatriz Garrido de la Reyes, Director General for Equal Treatment and Non-Discrimination and Against Racism at the Ministry of Equality of Spain, His Excellency Mr. James Dirangu Waweru, chair rapporteur of the intergovernmental working group on the effective implementation of the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action. And Ms. Katy Marcelo Lopez, president of the organization of Ashaninka indigenous women of the central Amazon region of Peru. Excellencies, distinguished participants, the list of speakers will close in 15 minutes. I encourage all speakers to intervene in an interactive way, present comments and ask questions that reflect the panelists' intervention and the discussion. I now have the honor to invite the Deputy High Commissioner for Human Rights to deliver her opening statement. Madam, you have the floor.

Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Excellencies, distinguished delegates. The Durban Declaration and Programme of Action is a global blueprint for racial justice and equality. Twenty-five years ago, it laid the foundation for much of today's international work against racial discrimination. It outlined wide-ranging measures to end racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia and related intolerance. It highlighted enslavement and colonialism as root causes of racism and looked ahead to global challenges, including widening inequalities and online hate. Today, we pay tribute to those who led the negotiation and the adoption of this landmark document. Civil society, particularly organizations led by people who experienced racism, played a central role. In the past 25 years, there has indeed been substantial progress towards addressing racism. The adoption or amendment of laws that prohibit racial discrimination, the adoption of national or regional policies, strategies and action plans, the establishment of equality bodies, and the adoption of a second decade on people of African descent. And yet, racism continues to poison communities, politics, media, sport, the online world and much more, and no country can claim to be free of it. Recent years have witnessed a resurgence of racist speech and actions, sometimes from the highest levels of government. Racist tropes rooted in white supremacy and harmful stereotypes are becoming normalised, including on social media. And some governments have taken actual steps to reverse anti-racist policies and initiatives. Many conflicts around the world are fueled by longstanding discrimination, dehumanization, and deepening inequality. Particularly severe forms of racial discrimination are at the heart of the protracted crises in Myanmar, in the occupied Palestinian territory, and Sudan, among others. Distinguished delegates, anti-Semitism, Islamophobia, and racism are surging around the world, while black migrants face pervasive forms of racism amid widespread anti-migrant vitriol. New data from 137 countries last year show that the most common form of discrimination is based on national or ethnic group, while discrimination on the basis of skin color remains prevalent. According to our own data, at least 30% of human rights defenders killed around the world in 2024 were indigenous or from a minority group. In European countries, black people, Roma, and people from different ethnic backgrounds continue to face racist harassment and racial discrimination, along with people targeted on account of their religious belief. At the global level, economic relations are shaped by power imbalances that reflect centuries of colonialism and exploitation. These inequalities affected and continue to affect global finance, trade and governance institutions. They do not reflect market efficiency, but rather policy decisions and frameworks that are in need of reform. Distinguished delegates, one of the lasting legacies of the D.D.P.A. and of the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination is the knowledge that racial discrimination, xenophobia, and related intolerance are not inevitable. They can be dismantled, but they require decisive leaders who take action at the individual, societal, institutional, and systemic levels. and by states and others that confront legacies of enslavement and colonialism and deliver reparatory justice. It requires strength and courage to shift stereotypes, challenge centuries of discrimination, dismantle power structures, and change behavior. In this regard, we need determined collective action. The simple way forward is for states to implement their commitments under the Durban Declaration and Plan of Action. This requires comprehensive reforms and responses and well-resourced national and regional action plans. It also requires data collection and disaggregation and independent monitoring by strong institutions. It requires educational reform and the participation of racial and ethnic groups in decision-making processes. And it requires accountability, access to justice, support for victims, and ways to repair the harm that was done, sometimes over generations. Businesses also have an important role. They have a responsibility to prevent and mitigate racial discrimination linked to their operations through policies, due diligence, and mechanisms to address grievances. They also play a key role at the community level by creating jobs and stimulating economic development. Media outlets have a specific role in promoting and reflecting diversity and fair representation, including in their coverage of culture and sports. And civil society organizations continue to be pivotal in pressing for systemic reform, identifying discrimination, advocating for justice and driving policy change. And I'm sure we'll hear more about the role of parliaments. But as civic space contracts, people and organizations that stand against racism are coming under increasing threat. Peaceful protesters on the streets, mothers fighting for justice for the deaths of their children and relatives, organizations working against hate and defending migrants' rights. We need to have each other's backs. Working in solidarity across equality movements amplifies our power and accelerates change. Real transformative action requires sustained and predictable funding, public recognition and support for these organisations. And our office provides guidance and technical expertise on anti-discrimination legislation, supports national action plans and strategies, data collection, education tools, and more that really encapsulate all the experience that we have in this area. We urge everyone to make full use of all of these. Distinguished delegates, Recent years have seen the loss of influential voices in the global struggle for civil rights and racial justice. Towering figures such as Desmond Tutu in South Africa, Marielle Franco in Brazil, and pioneers like Claudette Colvin and Jesse Jackson in the United States have shaped movements that transcended borders and inspired generations. Their legacies remind us that the pursuit of equality is shared across societies and rooted in many histories and diverse experiences. As we honor their memory, we must continue to find inspiration in their example. The UN Human Rights Office stands today and always with all who confront racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia, and related intolerance every day, everywhere. Thank you.

Thank you, Deputy High Commissioner. I will now give the floor to the distinguished panelists for their initial presentations. I have the honor to give the floor now to Mr. Martin Chungong. You have the floor, sir.

Thank you very much, Mr. President. Mr. President, Madam Deputy High Commissioner for Human Rights, distinguished panelists here on the podium, Your Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, it gives me great pleasure to be part of this conversation this morning. And indeed, I want to thank the Human Rights Council and the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights for inviting me on behalf of the IPU to join this conversation. I was asked during the preparations for this meeting to give you some initial reflections, personal reflections on the topic that we are addressing today. discrimination and racism. And I thought really hard, I asked myself what can I say from my own personal experience? And then it occurred to me that over the years as Secretary General, Head of the Inter-Parliamentary Union, when I do travel, people ask me, my interlocutors ask me in private, so where do you originally come from? Or they will say, oh, we hear you are the first African and non-European to be Secretary-General of the IPU. How do you feel about that? I do not say that this is overt racism or discrimination, but I do feel that the two are never far beneath the surface. And so it gives me pleasure today to reiterate the relevance of the Durban Declaration and Plan of Action that we are discussing today. And when I reflect on this, I realize that it was never intended as a time-bound response to a passing challenge. I think you have said it, Madam High Commissioner. Its relevance today is undeniable. Around the world, We are experiencing a resurgence of nativist rhetoric, persistent racial inequalities, the implication of hate speech online, and growing mistrust between communities. The manifestations may evolve, but the underlying challenge remains. The DDPA explicitly recognises the role of parliaments and the Inter-Parliamentary Union, and you asked me, Madam High Commissioner, to talk about the role of parliaments. Let me use this opportunity to highlight a few of those roles that accrue to parliaments and which are relevant to the declaration. One, parliaments pass legislation. they transform international commitments into binding national law. This includes enacting comprehensive anti-discrimination frameworks, criminalizing incitement to racial hatred, and addressing structural inequalities in education, employment, and access to justice. Yet, many parliamentarians encounter resistance when challenging entrenched interests and discriminatory narratives. Just this month, I had the pleasure of launching a new IPU study on violence against politicians, and we were amazed and overwhelmed to discover that more than 71% of MPs and politicians around the world reported having been victims of violence in one way or the other, online and offline. And so this is attributed to the fact that they address issues that are sensitive, such as racism and discrimination, and they are victimized on that account. And so we think that we need to move from rhetoric to political courage. you did say that fighting discrimination requires strong political courage, Madam Deputy High Commissioner. Second, I want to mention oversight. Parliaments have the role to oversee government, hold government accountable for the implementation of international commitments such as the Durban Declaration. And we are very keen for parliaments to exercise these powers, including ensuring that human rights institutions are properly resourced in the different countries. Then we have representation, inclusive institutions, strengthen public trust, and when parliaments reflect the diversity of the societies they represent or serve across race, ethnicity, religion, gender and age, they are better positioned to craft responsive and legitimate policies. Then I think parliaments have a strong role to play when it comes to leadership in public discourse. Parliaments shape national narratives at a time when racism and xenophobia can spread virally online. Elected officials have a particular responsibility to reject incitement, model respectful and fact-based debate, and show solidarity with those targeted by intimidation or stigma. We do not have at the IPU a stand alone programme on Durban, the Durban process, but combating discrimination is embedded in the DNA of the organisation and its current strategy. We work through our Committee on the Human Rights of Parliamentarians, we have capacity building initiatives, and we develop policy guidance that serve to support parliaments in addressing racism and related intolerance in practical and concrete ways. Credibility begins at home and leading by example is integral to our commitment to the values we promote. That is why the IPU's current strategy lays strong emphasis on representation and inclusive parliaments, including for groups that have historically been marginalized. Excellencies, let me conclude by pointing out that the DDP reminds us, and the Deputy High Commissioner also reiterated that, Combating racism requires coordinated efforts. It is not something to be left in the hands of one constituency alone. Governments, parliaments, civil society, the private sector and international organisations are all involved and should be involved. Parliaments play a key role in that galaxy and that ecosystem of stakeholders. I thank you, Mr. President, members of the Human Rights Council for this opportunity. I just want to reassure you that the IPU, the global organization of parliament, stands ready to continue to work with the Human Rights Council and other human rights advocates and stakeholders in upholding the provisions of the Durban Declaration. Thank you very much.
Thank you. Next, I have the honor to give the floor to Ms. Beatriz Carrio de los Reyes. Madam, you have the floor.

Good morning, Mr. President, High Commissioner, authorities, excellencies, dear colleagues, good morning. I would like to begin by expressing my gratitude for your invitation to participate in this panel representing the government of Spain. For me, as a person in charge of equal treatment policies and policies to combat racism, to be present here has a great deal of meaning, not just because of the institutional importance of this forum and the multilateral human rights system, but because of the the significant moment in history in which this event is taking place. 25 years after Durban, that is. The world, as we all know, is going through a complicated time of deep tension. There is more and more political polarization. Exclusive identity-based speech continues to gain ground in public debates. Hate speech finds new ways of gaining ground through digital means, and misinformation and bullies continue to erode coexistence and the most basic consensus and agreements. And in far too many cases, diversity is now seen as a threat. We are not confronted to isolated phenomena. This is a global struggle over the societal model that we want to defend and uphold. Durban came about at a time at which the international community understood that racism was not a single problem on the fringe. It understood that it was a structural problem that affects all countries. To combat it, meant more than moral condemnations. It called for public policies, cooperation among states, the participation of civil society, and political will sustained throughout time. Today we still have that same roadmap, as current today as it ever was, because contemporary racism is not merely seen explicitly. It is seen in persistent types of unequal access to housing, to employment, to justice, to education. And it is also seen in the over-representation of certain communities in situations of poverty and inequality. And particularly, it becomes seeped into the algorithms that double historic biases, and that will continue unless we have sufficient regulation. And on top of all of this, it has new forms that we must acknowledge, such as discrimination against people of African descent, against Roma people, against Arab, Muslim, indigenous peoples, and the list goes on, on top of institutional racism and the multiple types of exclusion that women of color continue to experience. The question is not whether Durban is still relevant today. The relevant question is whether we are enforcing it and whether we are doing enough. We in Spain, and please bear with me as I tell you what we are doing, we have learned that the fight against racism has an effect when it becomes part of the institutional architecture. which is why we have approved very strong laws such as the law on equal treatment and non-discrimination, which includes the inversion of the burden of proof and recognizes the principle of reparation offering stronger legal guarantees. We have created mechanisms for equal treatment in order to strengthen the institutional capability of oversight and legal support and assistance. And now we have bodies such as CEDRE, which is the Council for the Elimination of Racial Discrimination and Ethnic Discrimination. CEDRE has several offices across the Spanish territory, and we work in cooperation with ministries, institutions, with the different municipalities and civil society, because fighting racism cannot depend on political trends or individual wills. It needs structure, it needs investment, it needs support. Support coming by all people, all institutions, all stakeholders in society. We know that the progress we have made is not irreversible. In Europe and in some parts of the world, we are seeing, witnessing how extreme right political powers are using fear as a political weapon. We witness how certain types of speech are being repeated by the youth. We see how hatred is normalized online. And even through our screens in our pockets, we see how elsewhere in the world, small children are being held and separated from their parents, how people can break into someone's home, take the parents, leave the children behind, and put the parents into prison. This is not just a national phenomenon, it's transnational. Which is why defending Durban is defending multilateralism. It is defending the idea that human rights are not a concession with nothing, that it is a agreement among countries. a universal standard accepted by human rights. It is to assert that human dignity is non-negotiable. It is to believe that dignity strengthens rather than weakens our democracy. And if I may, I would like to add a personal note here. I am a Roma woman. I belong to a very large group that has survived centuries of persecution and attempted extermination, to be able to take the floor here today as a representative of a government is proof that institutions, when they do work, when they are democratic, can create opportunities of true equality. But it is not enough. We cannot be mere exceptions in spheres of power and participation. But this opportunity doesn't just happen spontaneously. It is the result of public policies, of historic memory, of inclusive education, and of strong legal frameworks. There can be no racial justice without memory. There can be no social cohesion without the effective participation of those who are involved in it. There can be no equality without resources. Durban gives us that clear framework. Cooperation in many levels, transformative education, effective access to justice, trustworthy data, support for victims, and real participation of the affected communities. Our job is to take that framework and turn it into tangible results, results that we can feel with our very own hands. Today, the world is facing many crises, geopolitical ones, economic, climate crises. Against that backdrop, one might be tempted to delegate the, relegate the anti-racism agenda to the back burner. That would be a very serious strategic mistake because racism is not a sectoral problem. It is a factor of social destabilization. It is important for social cohesion. It is an obstacle for the development of peoples and the development of our planet. To improve anti-racist policies does not erode our societies. Rather, it makes them stronger, more resilient. 25 years since Durban, the challenge now is not to redefine the problem, it is rather to renew the political agenda, to face it again much stronger still. We need international cooperation, we need more investment in education with a memory, with remembering the oppressed peoples. We need to improve the legal protection mechanisms, the accountability in digital platforms and to support this commitment beyond the electoral cycles. History has already showed us what happens when dehumanization becomes normal. We need look no further than just 80 years ago, how it all started and where we ended up. But it has also shown us that institutions, when they are backed by political will, can change the reality. And I will wrap up on this. Durban is not a historical document. It is our current compass to defend it today, is to defend the type of world that we want to pass on to future generations. Thank you.
Thank you, madam. Next, I have the honor to To give the floor to His Excellency Mr. James Dirangu Waweru. Sir, you have the floor.

Mr. President, it is an honor to address this high-level panel marking the International Day for Elimination of Racial Discrimination and commemorating the 25th anniversary of the adoption of the Durban Declaration and Programme of Work, the DDPA. I do this in my capacity as chair rapporteur of the intergovernmental working group on the effective implementation of the DDP, one of the central mechanisms established to follow up on the commitments made in Durban in 2001 and as a part of the wider UN anti-racism human rights architecture. 25 years on, the DDP remains the most comprehensive global framework for combating racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia, and related intolerance. Its breadth and scope continue to guide our collective understanding of racism as a structural, historical, and contemporary phenomenon rooted in legacies of slavery, the slave trade, including the transatlantic slave trade, colonialism, and systemic exclusion, and unfortunately persistent in modern institutions digital spaces, and socioeconomic inequalities. And it recognizes that racism manifests at the individual, community, and systemic levels, cutting across and also reinforced by other grounds of discrimination such as sex, gender, socioeconomic, health, and migration status. We must acknowledge the foresight and the depth of the DDPA. Durban drew an unbroken link between the past and the present, between slavery and the slave trade, including the transatlantic slave trade, and colonialism, and the enduring consequences of those atrocities today. It recognized that confronting these legacies requires not only acknowledgement, but also halting and reversing their lasting consequences, and addressing global structural inequalities importantly, The DDP-A recognized for the first time at a global level people of African descent as a distinct group and outlined specific measures needed to realize their rights. It also called for multi-stakeholder action at all levels, engaging not only states but also international financial institutions, the private sector, and even sports institutions. recognizing that dismantling systemic racism requires coordinated commitment across all sectors of society. Mr. President, as we commemorate the adoption of the DDP, we need to ask ourselves some pertinent questions. What, if evaluated, will be the grade of our fidelity to the provisions and aspirations of the Durban Declaration and Program of Action? What steps can we take to ensure that different actors across the spectrum collaborate effectively to accelerate progress and build the required momentum for the full implementation of the DDPA? Reflecting on these lessons learned, the UN anti-racism human rights mechanisms have highlighted progress since 2001. Public awareness has grown. There have been advances recognizing towards historical injustices. Efforts to strengthen the human rights framework on racial discrimination are underway, with progress being made in the development of the draft UN Declaration on the Rights of People of African Descent, and discussions on the elaboration of complementary standards to the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination continuing. However, this is not enough. Racial discrimination continues to be manifest in education, employment, health, housing, law enforcement and criminal justice systems, and now also in digital and algorithmic environments, which reproduce longstanding biases. Calls for reparatory justice and structural reforms as essential components for meaningful transformation are growing. Looking forward, Accelerating the implementation of the DDPA must be understood to be an absolute imperative to stem rising inequalities within and between countries and to prevent disunity and conflict and achieving its goals requiring renewed collaboration amongst all actors, states, UN entities and mechanisms. Combating racism is a collective and shared responsibility. Galvanizing political support against racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia and related intolerance requires a multi-layered holistic approach. The DDP provides precisely this through a clear practical roadmap. The owners then primarily lies with the state, which has the duty to act and enable actions by others. such as robust laws, strategies and action plans against racial discrimination, strong national human rights institutions and equality bodies. Mr. President, what we need today is stronger measures, greater implementation and more resources, broader support. The links to the key element of the DDPA, solidarity. Durban has taught us that confronting racism is not merely a national obligation, but a shared international responsibility. Both national and transnational solidarity are essential, especially as the challenges we face increasingly require coordinated multilateral responses and unity amongst all of us who are committed to fighting racism and inequality. This is what will enable us to translate commitments into tangible and lasting change. As Chair of the Intergovernmental Working Group, I reaffirm our mandate grounded in the DDPAs remains crucial. The DDPAs, as has been said, is a living document guiding us through the present and shaping our collective future and the world that we hope to leave to future generations. Implementing it fully means renewing our political will, strengthening our multilateral commitments and ensuring that every measure we take advances dignity, equality and justice for all. In closing, let the 25th anniversary of Durban not just be a moment of commemoration alone, but a moment of recommitment and decisive action towards a world where equality is a lived reality for all. The path ahead will not be easy, But it is one we must work together. I thank you.
Thank you. I have the honour now to give the floor to Ms. Katy Marcelo Lopez. Madam, you have the floor.

Good morning to all. We extend our greetings to you all and we thank the Human Rights Council. for inviting living voices to this panel. Twenty-five years on from Durban, the thoughts and the feelings of Latin America's indigenous women continue to see discrimination. We've seen 25 years since the Durban conference was adopted, 25 years since the international community recognized that racism and structural discrimination were open wounds in the history of humanity. And for us, the indigenous peoples and women of Peru and Latin America, Durban was not a symbolic act, but a response to the tireless struggle that started with our ancestors to seek respect for our equal dignity. In 2001, there was progress in international law with the adoption of the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of the Indigenous Peoples. But our collective rights continue to be violated. Racism has not gone. Structural discrimination is not dismantled when states like Peru reproduce the colonial heritage in their economic policy, promoting seizure of indigenous territories for extraction, criminalization of indigenous leaders who defend those lands which guarantee our lives. Latin America is the region where we see the most killings of indigenous leaders defending their lands. A lack of access to basic services such as intercultural health and bilingual education. And for indigenous women, the death is still higher. Indigenous women have defended their lands, transmitted our languages and our knowledge, protected our water and our lives. And yet we see triple discrimination as women, as indigenous people, and people living in lands that were historically excluded and impoverished by the ambitions of the elite. Our voices continue to be marginalized and silenced by decision makers. Our bodies have been subjected to violence and our children have been killed, leaving us in unbearable pain. Durban reminded us that racism is structural and the 25 years that have gone by show that this racism not only continues intact but it is also unpunished in our countries. When an indigenous girl goes to ordinary justice to get protected against sexual violence and contamination by HIV, the prosecutor of Peru sidelines those prosecutors who are obliged to investigate the perpetrators. When indigenous territories are invaded by the extractive industries without the state carrying out consultations or respecting our right to prior consent and our development model, that is structural racism. disclosure and the and delegitimization of our ancestral knowledge and the imposing of a single development model that destroys mother earth that is also structural racism. So interculturality is a response for state action on the existing gaps in cultural diversity, on historical, political and social issues where negative visions persist of diversity that feed discrimination, inequality and racism, particularly affecting the indigenous peoples and Afro-Peruvians. Interculturality is or should be dialogue, shared learning and exchange based on recognition of cultural differences. The intercultural approach is defined as adaptation of processes and services to geographical and environmental characteristics, as well as socio-economic, linguistic and cultural ones, with cultural practices, values and beliefs of the populations affected, which should value and incorporate the cosmic vision and development concepts of those peoples. We must emphasize the verbs adapt, value and incorporate because in practice what they try to do is include us, which means assimilate us. And the indigenous peoples and women don't want to be assimilated. We call for the exercise of our right to self-determination, for respect of our own way of life. We don't want to be reduced to folklore and stereotypes. because the republican states which began their lives 200 years ago on our continent continue to be colonial. And colonialism didn't end with independence. The policies of physical and cultural extermination continue with a systemic vulneration of the rights of the indigenous peoples and the Afro-Peruvians, with the gaps in gender, ethnicity and class in terms of exercise of rights. And this is our challenge. We must strengthen our organizations and link hands. to uphold our cultural identities and demand guarantees of the exercise of our rights, organize and join forces to end colonialism and change the system, create good living and full life. Indigenous women and Afro-descendant women in Latin America have suffered multiple structural violence and been part of the struggles in our lands. Thus, the need to continue building strategies for resistance and strengthening the paths of healing that are so badly needed. Racism is an important part of colonialism. It wasn't overcome by independence because republican states were created without the indigenous peoples and indeed against them. Racism in our countries is structural and heavily linked to classism. That's why we talk about class racism. For indigenous women, the discrimination is triple. There is no life free of violence without our ancestral lands. To protect indigenous women and guarantee our rights, we must guarantee the right to our lands for our peoples and our way of life. And that is the only way that we can do this through self-determination and indigenous autonomy. The gap, we must ensure that Durban goes beyond the laws. We need proper implementation. We must overcome colonial thinking. There are gaps between international standards and national law. This continues to be a major problem in our region. And yet we haven't come here as victims. We've come to bring the voice of the peoples and the indigenous women to tell you that we will continue to resist. we will continue to protect Mother Earth and all of the lives that depend on her. This is the heritage left to us by our ancestors and we will leave this to our children. What we want is to achieve respect of our equal dignity. 25 years on from Durban, the indigenous peoples and women tell you that it's not enough to recognize that racism exists, we must combat it. Durban was a starting point, 25 years on, it needs also to be a turning point. Thank you.

Thank you. I'd like to thank all members of the panel, excellencies, distinguished participants. We will now proceed with the first segment of the list of speakers. All interventions from the floor are limited to one minute and 30 seconds. And this, as you are aware, is due to cost-saving measures that we have all agreed to. The list of speakers is now closed. And I next have the honor to give the floor to the distinguished representative of South Africa. His Excellency.

Mr. President, distinguished delegates, At this historic juncture of the 25th anniversary of the Durban Declaration and the Programme of Action, we pay tribute to current and historical victims of racism and racial discrimination. In view of the persistence of this scourge, it remains pivotal that we assess progress in our collective efforts to combat it and rededicate ourselves to ensuring the full and effective implementation of the Durban Declaration and the Programme of Action Against Racism. The African Union theme for decades, namely, justice for Africans and people of African descent through reparations, remains our strategic rallying point for the realization of reparatory justice in this regard. We commend the African Union leadership for extending it from a year theme to a decade. We recognize the importance of the Second International Decade for Peoples of African Descent under the theme, The People of African Descent: Consideration, Justice and Development, and the need to galvanize global support to ensure the realization of reparatory justice. We are determined to unite in action to repair the gross human damage that was caused by colonialism, slavery, apartheid, slave trade, and the transatlantic slave trade. whose effects remain and whose pain and anger are still felt to date. I thank you.

I thank His Excellency Mr. Ronald Lamola, Minister of International Relations and Cooperation of South Africa. And next, I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Portugal, Her Excellency Ms. Ana Isabel Xavier, Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs and Cooperation of Portugal.

Thank you, President, distinguished Council Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen. It is an honour to address this high-level panel to celebrate the 25th anniversary of the adoption of the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action. 25 years on from adoption, these instruments continue to be the most comprehensive global framework against racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia and intolerance. Racism and racial discrimination, by their very nature, are not compatible with human dignity and equality. This anniversary is an opportunity to renew our collective efforts and transform commitments into action. For Portugal, combating racism and racial discrimination remain a national and international priority. Portugal remains strongly committed to full effective implementation of the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action. Thus, together with South Africa, Portugal facilitated the political declaration adopted at the 20th anniversary. In recent years, we've made important steps. Portugal adopted its first national plan of action to combat racism and discrimination. It created the Racism and Xenophobia Observatory. It carried out reform of the Commission on Equality and Against Racial Discrimination, making it independent, and it hosted the first in-person meeting of the anti-racism human rights defenders of the United Nations, contributing to coordination system and dissemination of good practice. And we know that the efforts must continue. There has to be ongoing coordinated action. You may always count on Portugal for that. Thank you.
Thank you. Next, I have the honor to give the floor to His Excellency, Mr. Festus Katuna Bandeka, Attorney General of Namibia.

Thank you, Mr. President, distinguished delegates. The Durban Declaration and the Program of Action is a living and present tool designed to tackle the enduring injustice of the past colonialism apartheid and inequality we still manifest in various ways across the world. As we mark the 25th anniversary of the near universal acceptance of the Durban Declaration, Namibia urges States to recommit to its principles. The slow progress in eliminating racism and racial discrimination worldwide requires universal action from all States. Mr. President, there is an urgent need to reinforce structural and socio-economic approach to implementing the Durban Declaration and political leadership is the critical conduit for the elimination of the racist and discrimination stereotypes and practices. Concrete measures aimed at implementing the recommendation of the Durban Declaration must be alive to the ever-changing dynamics of society in combating of discrimination and racist practices online and offline. States have an obligation to ensure that developers and operators access human rights due diligence in the entire technology lifecycle. The new and emerging technologies must be developed on principles of equality, merit-based assessment to avoid perpetuation of racial discrimination and racism in the use of populations. Furthermore, we underscore the importance of the role and technical assistance of the work of the Durban Declaration and the NIS and they both contribute to the implementation of the Declaration in different ways. Namibia remains committed to the full implementation of the Declaration and we maintain that prevention is the most effective way to eliminate racism and racial discrimination through collective interventions. I thank you.

Thank you. Next I have the honour to give the floor to Her Excellency Ms. Princess Kasune, Minister of Justice of Zambia. Can we provide the mic for the Minister of Zambia?
